scope: Manual proof/verifier inspection and independent exhaustive integer-divisor audit of every certificate row. This review does not cover later proof-note, video, phase-map or zeta-contour additions.

proof.lemma: If n is composite and n>=2, write n=ab with 2<=a<=b. Then a*a<=n. A prime divisor p of a satisfies p*p<=n. For n<=100, p<=10, so p is one of 2,3,5,7.
proof.primeCertificateRule: Every required trial prime p with p*p<=n has an exact nonzero remainder. The lemma excludes compositeness; n>=2 is checked separately.
proof.compositeCertificateRule: Exact integers d,q satisfy 1<d<n, 1<q<n and d*q=n.
proof.boundaryRule: 0 and 1 are neither prime nor composite.1 has one positive divisor and is a unit; a visualization switch must not silently relabel it prime.
proof.completeness: The verifier enforces exactly 101 ordered records, with row n containing exactly integer n, for every n from 0 through 100 inclusive.

checks.detail: Independently enumerated every proper integer divisor d=2..n-1, without calling generate(), and matched all 101 classifications.
Every prime row has exactly the required divisors from 2,3,5,7 under the inclusive integer test p*p<=n, with the exact positive remainder.
All 74 factor pairs are nontrivial and multiply exactly to their row integer.
49=7*7 is composite; 97 is prime; 100=2*50 is composite; 0 and 1 are neither.
Exact integer types exclude bools in row indices, factors and remainders; unsupported bounds, incomplete divisor coverage and false factors cannot verify.
The independent cross-check enumerates every proper divisor rather than reusing the four-prime generator. Its oracle prediction fixture is explicitly an evaluator test, not a predictor.
Seven additional malformed cases were independently submitted to verify(); all raised ValueError.

futureBrushTest: Freeze a computable color-to-prime rule and all rendering parameters before testing. Evaluate on a held-out range without supplying prime labels to the predictor. Compare forward/reverse draw order and resolution changes, or explicitly fix a canonical rendering; primality itself cannot depend on paint order.
limits: Elementary finite classification, not new mathematics, a proof-assistant artifact, or a result about zeta zeros or RH.
The certificate provides ground truth; it does not establish that brush colors predict primes.
The computational audit trusts Python integer arithmetic and the inspected verifier. The short divisor lemma supplies the mathematical justification.
